subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painful, fluctuant swelling at the posterior aspect of the vulvar vestibule. It began as a painless mass and became tender and erythematous over several days. She is sexually active and otherwise healthy.
question: Which of the following best explains this finding?

options.text: Blockage of a sebaceous gland duct with keratin accumulation
Blockage of the Bartholin gland duct with fluid accumulation and possible abscess
Chronic progressive inflammatory thinning of the vulvar skin
HPV-related squamous dysplasia of the vulva
Congenital failure of hymenal degeneration

explanation_correct: A Bartholin cyst results from blockage of the Bartholin gland duct with accumulation of gland fluid and is common in reproductive-age women. Obstruction with inflammation and infection can lead to a painful abscess. A tender, fluctuant mass at the posterior vestibule is the classic presentation.

explanation_incorrect.A: A sebaceous gland is not involved; the Bartholin gland is a mucus-secreting gland whose duct blockage produces this cystic swelling.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chronic inflammatory dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus produce porcelain-white plaques, not a fluctuant cystic mass of the vestibule.
explanation_incorrect.D: Vulvar squamous dysplasia or carcinoma presents with leukoplakia or a suspicious mass, not an acutely tender cystic swelling.
explanation_incorrect.E: Imperforate hymen causes primary amenorrhea with cyclic pain and hematocolpos, not a localized painful vulvar mass.

educationalObjective: Bartholin cyst/abscess results from blockage of the Bartholin gland duct with fluid accumulation, often in reproductive-age women; obstruction plus inflammation can produce an abscess.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Vulvar and vaginal pathology

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 6-year-old girl has intense vulvar itching and pain with urination and defecation. Examination shows porcelain-white atrophic plaques around the vulva and anus, producing a figure-eight pattern, with areas of hemorrhage and erosion.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Lichen simplex chronicus
Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma
Lichen sclerosus
Extramammary Paget disease
Bartholin abscess

explanation_correct: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic progressive inflammatory disease with porcelain-white plaques that may be hemorrhagic, eroded, or ulcerated. It can extend to the anus in a figure-eight pattern, occurs in prepubertal and peri-/postmenopausal females, and causes intense pruritus, dyspareunia, dysuria, and dyschezia. It is benign but carries a slightly increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lichen simplex chronicus is thick, leathery skin from chronic rubbing and lacks porcelain-white plaques and the perianal figure-eight distribution.
explanation_incorrect.B: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma occurs in postmenopausal women with leukoplakia, not in a young child with porcelain-white plaques.
explanation_incorrect.D: Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma with pruritus, erythema, and crusting or ulcers, typically in older patients.
explanation_incorrect.E: A Bartholin abscess is a painful cystic swelling of the vestibule, not atrophic porcelain-white plaques.

educationalObjective: Lichen sclerosus: chronic inflammation with porcelain-white plaques, figure-eight perianal involvement, intense pruritus, prepubertal/perimenopausal; benign but slightly increased SCC risk.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has a long history of vulvar itching and habitually rubs and scratches the area. Examination shows thick, leathery vulvar skin with accentuated skin markings. There are no porcelain-white plaques or ulceration. She asks whether this lesion can become cancerous.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition?

options.text: Benign squamous hyperplasia from chronic rubbing; no increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma
A premalignant lesion with a high rate of progression to invasive carcinoma
An intraepithelial adenocarcinoma with risk of an underlying invasive malignancy
A chronic inflammatory disease with porcelain-white plaques and a slight SCC risk
HPV 16/18-related vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia

explanation_correct: Lichen simplex chronicus is hyperplasia of vulvar squamous epithelium caused by chronic rubbing or scratching. It presents with leathery, thick skin with enhanced skin markings and is benign with no increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma. This contrasts with lichen sclerosus, which is associated with a slight increase in SCC risk.

explanation_incorrect.B: Lichen simplex chronicus is benign and is not a premalignant lesion with high malignant potential.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma describes extramammary Paget disease, not the hyperplastic, leathery lesion of lichen simplex chronicus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Porcelain-white plaques with a slight SCC risk describe lichen sclerosus, not this thick hyperplastic lesion from scratching.
explanation_incorrect.E: HPV-related vulvar neoplasia presents with leukoplakia and is driven by high-risk HPV, not by chronic rubbing.

educationalObjective: Lichen simplex chronicus is benign squamous hyperplasia from chronic rubbing—thick leathery skin with enhanced markings—and carries no SCC risk, unlike lichen sclerosus.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Vulvar and vaginal pathology

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 68-year-old woman has a persistent pruritic white patch on the vulva. Biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma. The pathologist notes two recognized etiologic routes to this tumor: infection with high-risk HPV and a long-standing inflammatory dermatosis.
question: Which of the following statements about vulvar carcinoma is correct?

options.text: It most often arises from a long-standing Bartholin gland cyst.
It is typically a clear cell adenocarcinoma arising from vaginal adenosis.
It is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that only rarely invades.
HPV types 16 and 18 and long-standing lichen sclerosus are both associated risk factors.
It commonly presents as a grapelike polypoid mass in young girls.

explanation_correct: Vulvar carcinoma is usually squamous cell carcinoma arising from the squamous epithelial lining of the vulva, most often in postmenopausal women presenting with leukoplakia. HPV-related vulvar carcinoma is associated with high-risk types 16 and 18, whereas non-HPV vulvar carcinoma usually arises from long-standing lichen sclerosus. Biopsy is often required to distinguish carcinoma from other causes of leukoplakia.

explanation_incorrect.A: A Bartholin cyst/abscess is a benign duct blockage and is not a precursor to vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.B: Clear cell adenocarcinoma from vaginal adenosis is a vaginal tumor linked to in-utero diethylstilbestrol exposure, not vulvar carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intraepithelial adenocarcinoma describes extramammary Paget disease, not invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva.
explanation_incorrect.E: A grapelike polypoid mass in a young child suggests sarcoma botryoides (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma), not vulvar carcinoma.

educationalObjective: Vulvar carcinoma is usually SCC in postmenopausal women (leukoplakia); HPV 16/18 and long-standing lichen sclerosus are the two main pathways.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 72-year-old woman has a chronic, itchy, erythematous, crusted and ulcerated plaque on the labia majora. Biopsy reveals large pale cells with mucin within the epidermis, consistent with intraepithelial adenocarcinoma. The patient is counseled about her risk of an underlying invasive cancer.
question: How does the risk of an underlying invasive malignancy in this vulvar condition compare with Paget disease of the breast?

options.text: It is the same as in breast Paget disease, where an underlying carcinoma is always present.
It is higher than in breast Paget disease because vulvar lesions frequently invade.
Neither condition has any malignant potential.
It is a squamous cell carcinoma in situ with a high invasive potential.
It is low risk for an underlying carcinoma, whereas breast Paget disease is always associated with underlying carcinoma.

explanation_correct: Extramammary Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that presents with pruritus, erythema, crusting, and ulcers. It is a carcinoma in situ with a low risk of an underlying carcinoma, in contrast to Paget disease of the breast, which is always associated with an underlying carcinoma. This distinction is a classic comparison point.

explanation_incorrect.A: In breast Paget disease an underlying carcinoma is always present; in extramammary Paget disease that risk is low, so the risks are not the same.
explanation_incorrect.B: Extramammary Paget disease is typically carcinoma in situ with a low risk of underlying carcinoma, not a high risk of invasion.
explanation_incorrect.C: Both conditions are neoplastic; extramammary Paget disease is an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, not a benign process.
explanation_incorrect.D: This is adenocarcinoma in situ, not squamous cell carcinoma in situ, and its invasive potential is low.

educationalObjective: Extramammary Paget disease is intraepithelial adenocarcinoma with low risk of underlying carcinoma; breast Paget disease is always associated with underlying carcinoma.
source: Generated from 15. Reproductive.pdf - Pathology: Vulvar and vaginal pathology

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 19-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding and a mass in the upper vagina. Her mother took diethylstilbestrol during pregnancy. Biopsy shows persistence of glandular columnar epithelium in the proximal vagina and malignant clear cells.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the vagina secondary to cervical SCC
Clear cell adenocarcinoma arising from vaginal adenosis
Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides)
Extramammary Paget disease of the vulva
Endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the uterine corpus

explanation_correct: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina arises from vaginal adenosis, the persistence of glandular columnar epithelium in the proximal vagina, and is strongly associated with in-utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES). The malignant clear cells and DES history in this patient make this the correct diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Vaginal squamous cell carcinoma is usually secondary to cervical SCC and is not linked to DES exposure or vaginal adenosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sarcoma botryoides affects girls under 4 years old with grapelike polypoid masses and desmin-positive spindle cells, not a DES-exposed teenager with adenosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Extramammary Paget disease is a vulvar intraepithelial adenocarcinoma causing pruritus and erythema, not a vaginal mass arising from adenosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Endometrioid adenocarcinoma arises in the uterine corpus and is not related to vaginal adenosis or DES exposure.

educationalObjective: Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina arises from vaginal adenosis (persistent glandular epithelium) in females exposed to diethylstilbestrol in utero.
